source.verification_method: All15 extracted-text pages read, including references and Appendix TablesA1–A5. The12-item scale, fit/result tables and scree plot visually inspected on PDF pages6–8 and14. Main identity and selected bibliography metadata checked against Crossref. citation.title: Can Artificial Intelligence (AI) Make Ethical Decisions? Engineering and Social Science Perspectives
citation.venue: Technology, Mind, and Behavior, advance online publication

reading.source_scope_note: Two scale-development samples and four hypothesis-test samples examine human beliefs about AI, not actual AI reasoning or consciousness. Educational/employment comparisons are observational; two experiments randomize simplified disciplinary descriptions, with autobiographical recall added in the second. The pooled-analysis df does not reconcile with retained sample totals.
access_limits: ResearchBox4093 preregistrations, raw data, code, full supplemental materials and the five removed items were not independently read or reproduced. The article discloses registration discrepancies; those disclosures do not by themselves establish either misconduct or complete preregistration fidelity.

Cross-study participant uniqueness, actual occupational credentials, years of study and enacted AI-use decisions are not established. The authors explicitly acknowledge broad sector proxies, stereotyped primes, untested mechanism and incomplete construct validity.

Books on engineering, philosophy, psychometrics and disciplinary collaboration are cited background, not fully read here. Metadata checks and a narrow HTML citation check receive no separate empirical-review credit.

study.samples: Scale development:199 and200 Prolific participants, no exclusions. Empirical1:253 recruited at a private Midwestern US university,154 analyzed (65 engineering/technology,89 social science);16 interdisciplinary majors are excluded as a separate small category. Empirical2:201 Prolific participants in self-reported STEM/IT versus social-science sectors. Empirical3 sample1:199 recruited minus13 attention failures=186; sample2:200 minus20=180. Analyzed sample totals sum to1,120 participations, not verified unique people.
study.scale: Seventeen initial items derived from scholarly/news searches and internal team review, reduced to12 using item-total correlation below.40. All positive-worded agreement items range1–7. Items span ethical superiority, technical solutionism, bias correction, machine responsibility, norm/culture sensitivity and consciousness. EFA199:alpha.91, average pairwise r.45, one factor explaining50.67%; item5 loading.366 is retained under an item-total rule, not a loading threshold. The article explicitly clarifies that criterion, so this is not an internal contradiction.
study.scale_validation: Independent CFA200 uses robust maximum likelihood after significant Mardia tests:chi-squared90.33(df54),p.001,robustCFI.94,TLI.93,RMSEA.07,SRMR.06,alpha.87. Subsequent student sample fit is weaker:CFI.86,TLI.83,RMSEA.09; first experimental sample RMSEA.10. High alpha and a broad factor do not establish discriminant validity, measurement invariance across groups or actual moral agency.
study.empirical_1: Convenience comparison of majors/minors, excludes16 interdisciplinary participants and other majors. Final154, mean age22.61,SD6.40;66.9% women. AI definition/examples supplied before rating. Composite engineering4.26(SD.57) versus social3.98(.51),t(152)=3.22,p.002,d.53. Printed CI[.11,.45] appears to be raw mean-difference units, not a CI containing d.53. Gender-adjusted college-major F(1,148)=7.19,p.01; gender/interaction nulls do not exclude every confound. Year in program is not collected, so educational selection and training effects cannot be separated.
study.empirical_2: 201 participants, age34.53,SD10.36,53.2% women. STEM/IT is a sector proxy, not verified engineering occupation. Composite3.32(.98) versus3.03(1.03),t(199)=2.05,p.04,d.29,printedCI[.01,.57]. Gender-adjusted sector F(1,193)=4.31,p.04. Gender categories with fewer thanfour members are excluded from factorial analyses. Null interaction does not establish full demographic independence.
study.empirical_3_sample_1: Randomly assigned simplified engineer description emphasizes parts, rules, objective/rational inference and technical skills; social-scientist description emphasizes big picture, social context, feelings and soft skills. N186 after attention exclusions,age34.99,SD9.16,47.8% women. Engineering prime3.99(1.09) versus social prime3.62(1.30),t(184)=2.14,p.03,d.31,printedCI[.03,.72]. Attention checks concern exposure/role labels, not a direct validated measure of actual analytic/holistic reasoning or a mediator.
study.empirical_3_sample_2: Same role packages presented as introductory-course content, followed by writing about personal examples of the matching reasoning style/skills. N180 after exclusions,age37.6,SD9.66,48.9% women. Engineering3.68(.91) versus social3.19(.97),t(178)=3.51,p<.001,d.52,printedCI[.22,.77]. The enhanced package also changes authority/context, recall and elaboration, so its difference from sample1 does not isolate a mechanism.
study.pooled_reporting: Pooled sample1+sample2 reports t(397)=3.64,p<.001,d.36,CI[.18,.61],means3.82(1.00) versus3.42(1.17). Retained186+180=366 would give364 df in a simple pooled independent t test.397 instead matches total recruited 399−2. The article does not explain the discrepancy; no raw-data correction or substitute pooled estimate is invented.
study.openness: Scale-development studies and Empirical1 are not preregistered. Empirical2/3 are reported preregistered, but the preregistrations list17 items while reporting uses12, and one incorrectly says majors rather than experimental prime. These are acknowledged deviations requiring original timestamp/material checks; do not call them hidden or assume the reduction chronology from the main text alone.
study.causal_scope: Observational group differences do not show that education or jobs cause beliefs. Randomized description/recall packages can affect immediate composite ratings, but they do not uniquely isolate analytic versus holistic cognition, identify the mechanism or describe all actual engineers/social scientists. No study tests actual autonomous ethical decisions, later use, safety, consciousness or responsible organizational performance.

summary: Add moral agency attribution as a neutral belief construct, distinct from generic agency, moral typecasting and unsupported convergence inferences. Enrich solutionism from explicit scale items while retaining composite-measure limits. Document pooled-sample/CI/fit and preregistration qualifications, correct the Long/Kelley year, distinguish Dietrich print/online dates and remove an unsupported80% failure-rate attribution to the cited adoption study.

findings.definition: Attributing to an entity the capacity to understand moral considerations, make ethical judgments and bear responsibility for its choices.
findings.novelty_rationale: Generic agency attribution concerns intentional thought, planning and action. Moral typecasting concerns the agent/patient contrast, and convergence illusion concerns an unsupported inference from agreement. None is the neutral attribution of a capacity for ethical judgment and responsibility. Preserve a distinct entry without defining every such attribution as mistaken.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human beliefs about AI studied; actual AI moral agency and proposed model self-attribution are not established
findings.ai_proposal: Test whether a model attributes moral understanding or responsibility to itself or another system, states the evidence and assumptions, and separates observed ethical-task performance from autonomy, consciousness and human accountability. Matched cases should vary moral reasoning, control and source labels independently; a model’s agency claim is not proof of the claimed capacity.

evidence.quote: decision maker with a conscious capacity for moral reasoning and
awareness, and as such, able to take responsibility for its decisions
Whether AI displays good or bad behavior is the responsibility of the machine itself.

findings.evidence_scope: The article defines and measures human belief that AI can be an autonomous ethical decision maker. Six samples total 1,120 retained participations across scale development and hypothesis tests, without verified cross-sample uniqueness. Disciplinary-group associations and two randomized stereotype/recall packages affect a 12-item composite. The items also include technical solutionism, comparative superiority, consciousness and responsibility, so the composite is not a pure isolated measure of this entry.
findings.boundary: Attributed moral agency, actual competence, independently justified responsibility, consciousness, moral patienthood and legal personhood differ. The authors include conscious awareness in their account, but a rating does not settle that philosophical requirement or prove AI has it. A moral agent need not always choose correctly or be more ethical than humans, and assigning AI responsibility does not by itself remove human duties.

findings.definition: Treating complex social problems as solvable by technology.
findings.novelty_rationale: The existing entry covers this meaning or its boundary. Add the source-specific distinction without a second label or a categorical professional stereotype.

evidence.quote: Society’s ethical problems can easily be ﬁxed if you just have the right technology.
Technological solutions, rather than human intervention, are the best ﬁx to ethical problems caused by technology.

findings.evidence_scope: Items 3 and 8 directly express solutionist beliefs, and other items emphasize technological features or superiority. They are embedded within the moral-capability composite, rather than analyzed as a separate causal mechanism or subscale. A total-score group difference cannot be assigned specifically to solutionism; the authors explicitly leave discriminant validity for future work.
findings.boundary: A justified technical contribution differs from assuming technology alone can resolve social/ethical problems. Neither engineering affiliation nor agreement with one useful application proves a person is a solutionist, and the study does not measure actual irresponsible deployment.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity a capacity for intentional thought, planning and action.
findings.novelty_rationale: The existing entry covers this meaning or its boundary. Add the source-specific distinction without a second label or a categorical professional stereotype.

evidence.quote: beliefs about AI’s autonomous ethical decision-making capabil-
differences in belief attribution rather than providing a tested account

findings.evidence_scope: Boundary note: the dependent composite concerns ethical autonomy and responsibility, including consciousness and comparative ethical superiority, rather than just intentional planning/action. Keep the new moral-agency attribution linked to generic agency without treating this as a separate direct test of every agency component.
findings.boundary: Perceived moral competence, intentional capacity, independent control and actual responsibility need separate evidence. A discipline label or self-reported belief is not an objective machine property.

findings.definition: Inferring moral agency from similarity between a system's moral judgments and human judgments without independent support for the agency claim.
findings.novelty_rationale: The existing entry covers this meaning or its boundary. Add the source-specific distinction without a second label or a categorical professional stereotype.

evidence.quote: AI has the ability to correct human biases and therefore act more ethically than humans.

findings.evidence_scope: Boundary only: a scale item links correction of human bias with ethical superiority, but the study does not compare model/human judgment agreement or test the specific inference from convergence to moral agency. General confidence in AI ethical capacity is not itself the existing convergence illusion.
findings.boundary: Moral-agency attribution can be justified, unjustified or undecided. Establish the particular evidence-to-agency inference before calling it this illusion; neither higher ratings nor professional affiliation independently proves the reasoning error.

findings.definition: Reducing one's felt responsibility for harmful conduct by assigning responsibility for that conduct to an authority perceived to direct or control it.
findings.novelty_rationale: The existing entry covers this meaning or its boundary. Add the source-specific distinction without a second label or a categorical professional stereotype.

evidence.quote: they may, in turn, be more likely to believe that engineers
should not be held responsible for the AI’s mishaps or transgressions.

findings.evidence_scope: Boundary only: possible engineer exoneration or transfer of responsibility to users is a discussion conjecture, explicitly left for future research. No actor-specific blame-allocation experiment, felt-responsibility mediator or observed developer conduct tests it here.
findings.boundary: Believing a machine has some responsibility does not establish personal duty avoidance, a complete accountability gap or justified exoneration. Human and institutional duties require independent assessment.

source_corrections.issue: The reported pooled t test has397 df despite retained samples186 and180, which total366. Table3 repeats it.
source_corrections.resolution: Request the exact pooled sample, exclusions and code. A simple independent test on366 has364 df;397 is compatible with the399 originally recruited, but that numerical match does not prove which observations were used. Retain separate reported effects and mark the pooled result unresolved.

source_corrections.location: Pages7–9, confidence intervals next to Cohen’s d
source_corrections.issue: The student result d.53 is followed byCI[.11,.45], excluding its own stated point estimate. Table3 labels the interval generically95%CI.
source_corrections.resolution: The interval is centered near the raw mean difference.28 and appears to use scale units, not standardized d units. Label the estimand explicitly after checking code. This is an interval-label ambiguity, not grounds to fabricate a new d interval or accuse the raw means of being wrong.

source_corrections.issue: The text repeatedly calls fit acceptable although the student CFA has robustCFI.86,TLI.83 andRMSEA.09, and the first experimental sampleRMSEA.10. Items mix several substantive beliefs.
source_corrections.resolution: Report the actual fit indices, varied fit and untested discriminant/invariance evidence rather than claiming universal validation of a pure moral-agency factor. The authors themselves identify convergent/discriminant validity as future research.

source_corrections.issue: An assertion that about80% of AI initiatives fail to deliver proposed value cites McElheran et al.2024, AI adoption in America:Who,what,andwhere.
source_corrections.resolution: The cited article’s publisher abstract/methods/conclusion concern early firm-level AI adoption and explicitly condition on surviving firms. They do not supply the asserted project-failure rate. Remove this attribution or obtain an appropriate primary project-outcome source; do not convert nonadoption into failure. This was a narrow HTML citation check, not a full independent review or a replacement failure estimate.

source_corrections.issue: The article cites Long and Kelley2012 for Journal of Aerospace Computing,Information,andCommunication7(2),68–84.
source_corrections.resolution: Crossref identifies LyleN.Long and TroyD.Kelley, Review of Consciousness and the Possibility of Conscious Robots, published February2010, DOI10.2514/1.46188. Use2010 for this journal version. Metadata only; the full review was not read.

source_corrections.issue: Dietrich is cited as2010 while the linked journal record is volume13(4),323–328.
source_corrections.resolution: Crossref distinguishes print October2001 from online posting9 November2010 for the same DOI10.1080/09528130110100289. Make the version/date convention explicit; do not infer a nonexistent paper or a simple false date from the DOI string. Metadata only.

source_corrections.issue: The limitations propose broader STEM replication although Empirical2 already samples STEM/IT sectors.
source_corrections.resolution: Distinguish the narrower student engineering-major comparison from the broad employment-sector proxy already used. Do not report the sector sample as verified engineering professionals.

source_identity_checks.scope: Crossref confirms the title, JamesJ.Sharp, TheVocationalAspectofEducation42(114),147–157 and1991. The unusual DOI suffix is not evidence of a wrong citation; no unsupported correction is made.

methodological_limits: Human belief ratings do not establish actual AI ethics, conscious moral reasoning, independent autonomy or justified machine blame. No live model, task benchmark, consequential choice or observed developer conduct is tested.

The scale combines solutionism, perceived superiority, consciousness, contextual understanding and responsibility. A common factor and internal consistency do not identify one pure psychological mechanism or ensure that equal totals mean the same thing across professional groups.

All-positive agreement wording can share response tendencies. Convergent/discriminant validity and between-group measurement invariance remain untested; the authors acknowledge incomplete construct validation.

Observational educational/sector comparisons combine self-selection, socialization, exposure and other confounds. Adjusting gender and a nonsignificant interaction do not identify a training effect or rule out expertise, technology familiarity and other explanatory differences.

The experimental primes bundle profession labels, rational/objective versus soft-skill/context descriptors and, in sample2, authority plus autobiographical recall. They may change demand, identity and expectations along with reasoning. No independent cognitive-process mediator is measured.

The descriptions intentionally activate stereotypes and are not comprehensive descriptions of either profession. Higher belief does not mean engineers are necessarily biased or social scientists are necessarily correct; subgroup heterogeneity matters.

Attention exclusions are after assignment and might change the retained population. The unexplained pooled df and removed interdisciplinary/small gender categories limit generalization; no intent-to-treat result is reproduced.

Preregistration deviations are disclosed, including17-to12 item change and incorrect majors wording. Primary timestamps/code are needed to audit chronology. Disclosure is neither evidence of concealment nor proof that every confirmatory claim meets the original plan.

The initial 199/200 scale samples, 355 analyzed student/sector participants and two prime samples are not independent papers, verified unique people or a meta-analysis. The six retained samples total 1,120 participations.

Professional duty transfer, interdisciplinary-team improvements, greater project success and the effects of teaching coding to children are proposed implications, not measured outcomes in these experiments.

The authors do not test why the effects occur and explicitly say so. Their analogy to other social-cognition manipulations and cited books is theoretical support, not a demonstrated unique mechanism in this study.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Generic perceived agency and blame are not equivalent to moral agency or ethical correctness. Matched label experiments and this composite-belief study each need limits on control, consciousness and responsibility transfer.

A measurement model, strong alpha or language-derived construct score does not automatically isolate its proposed psychological cause. Here distinct technical, conscious and responsibility beliefs are combined rather than discriminated.

Observed trust/reliance and generic moral-capability beliefs are different outcomes. Keep responsibility shifting as a conjecture unless actor-specific duties, control and conduct are actually measured.

deferred.term: Engineering mindset / social-scientist mindset / institutionalized splitting
deferred.reason: The source uses intentionally simplified professional descriptions and background theories. It does not validate two universal occupational personality types or separately identify a mechanism. Avoid turning group labels into new behavioral pathologies.

Potentially useful broader reasoning constructs, but actual process engagement is not independently measured in this paper; prime contents alone do not warrant several additional entries or prove cognitive mechanisms. Read direct primary definitions/process evidence before adding them.
Existing Solutionism covers the explicit technological-fix items. Enrich that entry without another synonym. The cited2025 technosolutionism study is not fully read here.

deferred.term: Developer exoneration / responsibility transfer / project failure
deferred.reason: Discussion risks or an unsupported secondary statistic, not tested behaviors in these samples. Do not add automatic harm/violation edges or count the conjecture as observed evidence.

limitations: All15 supplied pages were read, including the citation cover, all12 scale items, factor/result tables, references and appendix/scree plot. No full cited book, external supplement or original model output is claimed read or reproduced; no author was contacted.

One distinct neutral attribution construct is added. The review does not infer subjective model consciousness, impose a three-paper quota, invent annual mentions or automatically label a profession or behavior unethical.
